blocks.text: 2.5.2. Permitted and Non-Permitted Subclasses in Sealed Classes and Interfaces
Overview

Sealed classes and interfaces in Java allow you to restrict which classes can inherit from them. This feature provides more control over the class hierarchy and enables better code organization and maintainability. In this section, we'll explore permitted and non-permitted subclasses in the context of sealed classes and interfaces.
Key Concepts
Permitted Subclasses

items: Explicitly listed classes that are allowed to extend a sealed class or implement a sealed interface.
Defined using the `permits` keyword in the sealed class or interface declaration.
Must be in the same module as the sealed class or interface, or in the same package if the sealed type is in an unnamed module.

blocks.text: Non-Permitted Subclasses

items: Classes that are not allowed to extend a sealed class or implement a sealed interface.
Any attempt to create a non-permitted subclass will result in a compilation error.

blocks.text: Declaring Permitted Subclasses
There are two ways to declare permitted subclasses, and they cannot be mixed:

items: **Explicit Declaration**: Using the `permits` clause in the sealed class or interface declaration.

items.text: public sealed class Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle { }

items: **Implicit Declaration**: When the permitted subclasses are defined in the same file as the sealed class or interface.
**No Mixed Declaration**: Once a `permits` clause is present, it is the complete list; a subclass in the same file that is not listed is rejected.

blocks.text: Rules for Permitted Subclasses

items: Permitted subclasses must extend the sealed class or implement the sealed interface.
Permitted subclasses must be declared as either `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
Permitted subclasses must be accessible to the sealed class or interface.

blocks.text: Benefits of Using Permitted Subclasses

items: **Type Safety**: Ensures that only specific classes can inherit from a sealed type.
**Code Maintainability**: Provides a clear and controlled hierarchy of classes.
**Pattern Matching**: Enables exhaustive pattern matching in switch expressions.
**API Design**: Allows for better API design by controlling extensibility.

blocks.text: Common Pitfalls

items: Forgetting to declare permitted subclasses as `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
Attempting to create a subclass that is not permitted.
Declaring permitted subclasses in a different package or module (when not allowed).

blocks.text: Best Practices

items: Use sealed classes and interfaces when you want to restrict the inheritance hierarchy.
Choose the appropriate modifier (`final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`) for permitted subclasses based on your design needs.
Keep the list of permitted subclasses minimal and focused on the domain model.
Use sealed classes in combination with pattern matching for more robust switch expressions.

blocks.text: Interview Insights

items: Be prepared to explain the difference between `sealed`, `final`, and `non-sealed` classes.
Understand the implications of sealed classes on class design and inheritance.
Be able to discuss scenarios where sealed classes provide benefits over traditional class hierarchies.

blocks.text: Q: How does using sealed classes and interfaces improve pattern matching in switch expressions?

A: Sealed classes and interfaces improve pattern matching in switch expressions by enabling exhaustive pattern matching. Since the compiler knows all possible subclasses of a sealed type, it can ensure that all cases are covered in a switch expression. This leads to more robust and maintainable code.

Q: What is the difference between `final`, `sealed`, and `non-sealed` subclasses of a sealed class?
A: The differences are:

items: `final` subclasses: Cannot be extended further. They are the end of the inheritance chain.
`sealed` subclasses: Can be extended, but only by their own permitted subclasses. This creates a multi-level sealed hierarchy.
`non-sealed` subclasses: Can be freely extended by any class, effectively "opening up" the hierarchy at that point.

blocks.text: Example:
Q: What are some common pitfalls when working with sealed classes and interfaces?
A: Common pitfalls include:

items: Forgetting to declare permitted subclasses as `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
Attempting to create a subclass that is not permitted.
Declaring permitted subclasses in a different package or module (when not allowed).
Overusing sealed classes, which can lead to overly rigid class hierarchies.
Not considering the impact on future extensibility of the codebase.

blocks.text: To avoid these pitfalls:

items: Always declare the permitted subclasses with the appropriate modifier.
Keep the sealed class and its permitted subclasses in the same package or module.
Use sealed classes judiciously, balancing control over the class hierarchy with flexibility for future changes.
Consider using interfaces or abstract classes for more flexible designs when appropriate.
